description: CONTROL TYPE | Identifies and alerts on security incidents during or after they occur, relying on monitoring and review rather than prevention. Examples: IDS, SIEM alerts, log monitoring, security audits, CCTV review.

CONTROL TYPE | Acts after an incident to limit its impact and restore systems or data to their normal state. Examples: restoring from backups, patch management, IPS blocking active attacks, disaster recovery procedures.

CONTROL TYPE | An alternative safeguard used when the primary control is too costly or impractical to implement, providing similar protection through other means. Example: extra logging and monitoring on a legacy system that cannot be patched or encrypted.

CONTROL TYPE | Specifies acceptable behavior and directs personnel toward secure practices through policy rather than technical enforcement. Examples: acceptable use policies, security awareness training, warning signage.

CONTROL CATEGORY | Administrative controls implemented through policies, procedures, and governance to manage organizational risk. Examples: risk assessments, security policies, security awareness programs, vendor due diligence.

CONTROL CATEGORY | Controls carried out primarily by people (rather than systems) as part of day-to-day operations to maintain security. Examples: security guards, incident response procedures, configuration management, user training.
CONTROL CATEGORY | Controls implemented through technology and systems to enforce security requirements. Examples: firewalls, encryption, access control lists, multifactor authentication, IDS/IPS.

ZERO TRUST | The policy-decision layer of a Zero Trust architecture; it evaluates every access request before granting entry rather than trusting anything by default. Uses adaptive identity, which continuously verifies a subject using contextual signals (location, device posture, behavior, risk score) instead of a single one-time login, alongside threat scope reduction and policy-driven access control enforced by the policy engine and policy administrator.

ZERO TRUST | Control Plane component that evaluates real-time risk indicators—such as user behavior, device health/posture, geographic location, and connection type—rather than relying solely on static credentials.
ZERO TRUST | Control Plane component that grants or denies access using explicit rules mapped to roles, context, and risk instead of trusting an internal network segment.
ZERO TRUST | Control Plane component acting as the "judge" that analyzes the incoming access request against security policies and context data to make the core allow/deny decision.
ZERO TRUST | Control Plane component acting as the "bailiff" that executes the Policy Engine's decision, coordinates connections, and issues session tokens.
ZERO TRUST | Data Plane component that intercepts traffic and enforces the decision handed down by the control plane (Policy Engine and Policy Administrator).

ZERO TRUST | Control Plane principle that minimizes the attack surface and "blast radius" via micro-segmentation, least-privilege access, and the assumption that a breach has already occurred (assume breach).
